findings.lesson_title: The Catholic threat: Northern Earls, plots and Mary Queen of Scots
findings.claim: About 450 rebels were executed — a deliberately harsh response to deter future revolt.
findings.issue: The number of rebels executed after the Northern Rebellion is understated. Historical sources consistently put the figure at approximately 600, with Elizabeth having demanded at least 700. The figure of 450 is significantly below the scholarly consensus.
findings.correction: Approximately 600 rebels were executed following the suppression of the Northern Rebellion (Elizabeth demanded at least 700; estimates range from 400 to over 600, with ~600 being the most widely cited figure).

findings.lesson_title: The need for social reform: Booth, Rowntree and Liberal reforms
findings.claim: Part 1 provided sickness benefit — 10 shillings per week for up to 26 weeks — to some 10 million workers who were ill.
findings.issue: The 10 shillings per week rate did not apply for the full 26 weeks. Under the National Insurance Act 1911, sickness benefit was 10 shillings per week for the first 13 weeks, then reduced to 5 shillings per week for the following 13 weeks (total 26 weeks). Stating 10s/week for the full 26 weeks overstates the benefit rate and could lose marks in an exam answer.
findings.correction: The sickness benefit was 10 shillings per week for the first 13 weeks of illness, then 5 shillings per week for the next 13 weeks (26 weeks total).
findings.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Insurance_Act_1911; multiple sources confirm the two-tier rate structure

findings.lesson_title: The Spanish Armada
findings.claim: In 1587, Drake launched a pre-emptive raid on Cadiz harbour, destroying approximately thirty Spanish ships being prepared for the Armada.
findings.issue: The number of Spanish ships destroyed at Cadiz is slightly understated. Britannica records 33 ships destroyed; the Library of Congress source (based on Drake's own account) records 37. 'Approximately thirty' is at the low end and arguably inaccurate.
findings.correction: Drake destroyed approximately 33–37 Spanish ships at Cadiz in April 1587 (Britannica: 33; Library of Congress: 37). 'Over thirty' would be more accurate than 'approximately thirty'.

findings.lesson_title: The Spanish Armada
findings.claim: Of the approximately 130 ships that set out, only around 67 returned to Spain.
findings.issue: The number of Armada ships returning to Spain is slightly overstated. Wikipedia and the majority of modern scholarship puts the figure at approximately 60–65 ships returning, not 67.
findings.correction: Approximately 60–65 ships returned to Spain (Wikipedia records 'about 60 known to have reached Spain'; contemporary Spanish records cite 65 survived). 67 is slightly high.

findings.lesson_title: Culture and fashion in Edwardian Britain
findings.claim: Beatrix Potter published The Tale of Peter Rabbit in 1902, initially self-published after Frederick Warne accepted it the same year.
findings.issue: The publication sequence is confused. Potter self-published a private edition of 250 copies in December 1901 (not 1902), after multiple publishers rejected the manuscript. Frederick Warne then accepted and published the first commercial trade edition in October 1902. Saying she self-published 'after' Warne accepted it 'the same year' inverts the order: she self-published first (1901), Warne published second (1902).
findings.correction: Potter privately printed 250 copies in December 1901 after publishers rejected it. Frederick Warne & Co. then published the first commercial edition in October 1902. The self-publication preceded (and prompted) the Warne commercial deal, not vice versa.

findings.lesson_title: The end of austerity: 'never had it so good'
findings.claim: Wilson created a new Ministry of Technology and increased funding for higher education, overseen by a major expansion of universities following the Robbins Report of 1963 (which recommended expanding university places from around 130,000 to 350,000).
findings.issue: The Robbins Report figures are significantly wrong. At the time of the report (1962/63), there were approximately 216,000–238,000 full-time students in higher education in Great Britain. The report recommended expanding places to approximately 558,000 by 1980/81 — not from 130,000 to 350,000. Both the baseline and the target in the lesson are substantially incorrect.
findings.correction: The Robbins Report (1963) recommended expanding full-time higher education places from approximately 216,000 (at the time of the report) to approximately 558,000 by 1980/81.

findings.lesson_title: Immigration: Windrush, race riots and Enoch Powell
findings.claim: Out of the Notting Hill riots came, indirectly, the Notting Hill Carnival, founded in 1965 as a community-building response to the violence
findings.issue: The year 1965 is incorrect. The first outdoor Notting Hill Carnival took place in August 1966, organised by Rhaune Laslett as a street festival for neighbourhood children. An indoor Caribbean Carnival was held from 1959 by Claudia Jones at St Pancras Town Hall. Neither date is 1965. Sources consistently give 1966 as the start of the outdoor street carnival that became the annual Notting Hill Carnival.
findings.correction: The Notting Hill Carnival's outdoor street format began in 1966 (organised by Rhaune Laslett). An earlier indoor 'Caribbean Carnival' was established by Claudia Jones from 1959. The year 1965 is not supported by historical sources.

findings.lesson_title: Changing attitudes to authority: the permissive society
findings.claim: CND's first Aldermaston march took place at Easter 1958; it attracted an estimated 4,000 marchers from London to Aldermaston. By the early 1960s the march reversed direction (Aldermaston to London)
findings.issue: The reversal of direction happened from 1959, not the 'early 1960s'. The 1958 march went from London to Aldermaston (organised by the Direct Action Committee, supported by CND). From 1959 onwards CND organised the annual march in the reverse direction — Aldermaston to London — to direct attention at Parliament. Saying 'early 1960s' implies it reversed around 1960–62 when it actually reversed in 1959.
findings.correction: The march direction was reversed from 1959 (not the early 1960s). The 1958 march (London to Aldermaston) was the only one in that direction; all subsequent CND-organised marches ran Aldermaston to London from Easter 1959 onwards.

findings.lesson_title: Civil unrest in Northern Ireland
findings.claim: The death toll for 1971 was 180; for 1972, the worst year of the Troubles, it rose to approximately 470 deaths.
findings.issue: The 1971 figure of 180 is wrong. The CAIN/Wesley Johnston annual death statistics for the Troubles record 171 deaths in 1971, not 180. The 1972 figure of 'approximately 470' is broadly defensible (the actual figure is 476 by the same dataset), so the 1972 figure does not require correction.
findings.correction: The death toll for 1971 was 171 (per the Malcolm Sutton index as recorded in the CAIN database). The 1972 figure of approximately 470 is broadly accurate (actual: 476).

findings.lesson_title: Racial policy: Nazi treatment of the Jews to 1939
findings.claim: around 400 synagogues were burned
findings.issue: The figure of 'around 400 synagogues' does not appear in any major authoritative source. The USHMM cites either 267 synagogues specifically confirmed burned/destroyed during the two-night pogrom itself, or 'more than 1,400 synagogues' damaged/destroyed across the broader area including Austria and the Sudetenland. The '400' figure is unsupported and falls between both established figures without matching either.
findings.correction: Authoritative sources give two figures: 267 synagogues confirmed burned or destroyed (USHMM specific count for Germany), or more than 1,400 synagogues damaged or destroyed across Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland (USHMM broader count). The lesson should use one of these established figures, e.g. 'more than 1,400 synagogues were attacked or destroyed' or 'around 267 synagogues were burned to the ground'.

findings.lesson_title: Prohibition and organised crime
findings.claim: On 16 January 1920, Prohibition came into force across the United States.
findings.issue: January 16 is the date the Eighteenth Amendment was ratified (1919), not when Prohibition came into force. Prohibition actually came into force on January 17, 1920, under the terms of the Volstead Act, which set the operative date as one year after ratification (i.e. 17 January 1920). A student writing '16 January 1920' in an exam would be giving a wrong date for when Prohibition started.
findings.correction: Prohibition came into force on 17 January 1920. The Eighteenth Amendment was ratified on 16 January 1919; the Volstead Act set the enforcement start date one year later, at midnight beginning 17 January 1920.

findings.lesson_title: The 1920s economic boom
findings.claim: The cost of a Model T fell from $825 in 1908 to $260 by 1925
findings.issue: The 1908 price of the Model T is given as $825 but the established historical figure is $850. Multiple sources including Britannica, Ford Motor Company records and the Library of Congress give the 1908 launch price as $850. The $260 figure for 1925 is correct.
findings.correction: The Model T cost $850 in 1908 (not $825), falling to $260 by 1925.

findings.lesson_title: Weimar Germany, 1919-1933: a survey
findings.claim: reparations set at £132 billion in 1921
findings.issue: The currency unit is wrong. Reparations were set at 132 billion gold marks (not pounds sterling). 132 billion gold marks was equivalent to approximately £6.6 billion or $33 billion USD at 1921 values. Stating '£132 billion' overstates the figure by a factor of roughly 20 and confuses the currency. GCSE students could lose marks quoting this.
findings.correction: Reparations were set at 132 billion gold marks in May 1921 (the London Schedule of Payments). This was equivalent to approximately £6.6 billion pounds or $33 billion USD at the time.

findings.lesson_title: Rise and consolidation of Nazi power, 1933-1934
findings.claim: The purge — known as the Night of the Long Knives — killed approximately 85 to 200 people
findings.issue: The lower bound of '85' refers to the announced/Gestapo list figure; the upper bound of '200' is one estimate. However, most modern historical scholarship gives higher estimates: Britannica and Wikipedia note that unofficial estimates put the death toll well above 200, with some estimates reaching several hundred. The lesson's '85 to 200' range, while not entirely wrong, understates the scholarly consensus range which commonly extends to 400+. As a secondary concern, the lesson elsewhere says 'Approximately 5,000 people were arrested' in the July Plot context (different lesson) — this is addressed separately.
findings.correction: Casualty estimates for the Night of the Long Knives range from a minimum of 85 (the announced Gestapo figure) to estimates of several hundred; the precise total remains disputed. '85 to 200' is defensible but on the conservative end.

findings.lesson_title: Life during the Second World War
findings.claim: Approximately 5,000 people were arrested in the subsequent purge; around 200 were executed, including Stauffenberg.
findings.issue: The arrests figure is significantly understated. USHMM, Britannica, Wikipedia, and multiple other authoritative sources state that approximately 7,000 people were arrested following the July Plot. The ~5,000 figure is closer to the number executed (approximately 4,980 executed), not the number arrested. The lesson conflates these two figures: it says 5,000 arrested and 200 executed, when in fact ~7,000 were arrested and ~4,980 were executed. The '200 executed' figure only captures the inner circle of direct conspirators, not the full reprisal purge.
findings.correction: Approximately 7,000 people were arrested in the aftermath of the July Plot. Of these, an estimated 4,980 were executed — not around 200. The '200' figure represents only the most prominent direct conspirators. The full reprisal purge was far larger.

findings.lesson_title: West Germany: economic recovery and politics
findings.claim: By 1973 approximately 2.6 million Turks were living in West Germany
findings.issue: The 2.6 million figure for Turkish residents applies to approximately the mid-2000s, not 1973. Between 1961 and 1973 around 867,000 Turkish guest workers travelled to Germany, of which around 500,000 returned, leaving roughly 600,000-900,000 Turkish nationals in West Germany by the time recruitment ended in 1973. The 2.6 million figure is around three times too high for 1973 and could seriously mislead students. The 2.6 million total Gastarbeiter (all nationalities) by 1973 is more plausible but conflates all nationalities with Turks specifically.
findings.correction: By 1973 approximately 600,000-900,000 Turkish nationals were living in West Germany (not 2.6 million). The Turkish population reached around 2.4-2.6 million only by the mid-2000s. The total Gastarbeiter from all countries combined peaked at around 2.6 million by 1973, which may be the source of confusion.

findings.lesson_title: The Berlin Wall and Cold War relations
findings.claim: Kennedy visited West Berlin and addressed a crowd of approximately 450,000 people at the Rudolph-Wilde-Platz
findings.issue: The 450,000 figure refers to estimates of people lining the streets of West Berlin during Kennedy's entire visit, not specifically to the crowd at Rudolph-Wilde-Platz (Rathaus Schöneberg). The crowd at Rudolph-Wilde-Platz where Kennedy delivered the 'Ich bin ein Berliner' speech is most commonly cited at around 120,000. Attributing 450,000 specifically to the square is misleading.
findings.correction: Approximately 120,000 people gathered at Rudolph-Wilde-Platz (Rathaus Schöneberg) for Kennedy's speech on 26 June 1963. The 450,000 figure (or higher estimates of 1.1 million) refers to total crowds lining the streets of West Berlin during his entire visit, not the specific plaza audience.

findings.lesson_title: Division of Germany, 1945-1961
findings.claim: Between 1949 and 1961 approximately three million East Germans left
findings.issue: Most authoritative sources give a higher figure of approximately 3.5 million (Berlin Wall Foundation, Britannica) to 3.8 million East Germans who emigrated between 1949 and 1961. 'Approximately three million' understates the commonly cited figure by half a million to nearly a million, which matters for students asked to provide precise statistics.
findings.correction: Between 1949 and 1961 approximately 3.5 million East Germans emigrated to the West (some sources give up to 3.8 million). 'Approximately three million' is an underestimate.

findings.lesson_title: Reunification, 1989-1991
findings.claim: Between 1949 and 1961 approximately three million East Germans had emigrated to the West
findings.issue: Same issue as Germany L5: the figure should be approximately 3.5 million (consensus of authoritative sources), not three million. This second instance of the same understatement reinforces the need for correction.
findings.correction: Approximately 3.5 million East Germans emigrated to the West between 1949 and 1961. Multiple authoritative sources (Berlin Wall Foundation, Britannica, Wikipedia) consistently give this higher figure.

findings.lesson_title: Life during the Second World War
findings.claim: The firebombing of Hamburg in July–August 1943 (Operation Gomorrah) killed an estimated 37,000 people
findings.issue: Casualty estimates for Operation Gomorrah vary significantly across authoritative sources: the most commonly cited range is 34,000–40,000 (Hamburg city archives, World History Encyclopedia), with some sources giving figures up to 46,000 or higher. The lesson's '37,000' figure is defensible but is stated definitively when historians note it is contested. More importantly, it is on the lower end and slightly below the most widely cited figure of approximately 40,000. Presenting a precise figure without noting the uncertainty is slightly misleading.
findings.correction: Casualty estimates for Operation Gomorrah (July–August 1943) range from approximately 34,000 to 46,000 killed, with most sources citing figures around 37,000–40,000. The exact number cannot be determined with certainty.

findings.lesson_title: Division of Germany, 1945-1961
findings.claim: at the airlift's peak, one plane landed every 90 seconds
findings.issue: The peak frequency of Berlin Airlift landings was one plane every 45 seconds (at Tempelhof airport during the 'Easter Parade' of April 1949), not every 90 seconds. Multiple sources including the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum and other authorities cite 45 seconds as the peak interval. The 90-second figure may reflect an average during normal operations rather than the peak.
findings.correction: At the peak of the Berlin Airlift (Easter 1949), one aircraft landed at Tempelhof every 45 seconds. The 90-second figure appears to be an average rather than the peak.

findings.lesson_title: The Great Depression and the New Deal
findings.claim: When around 20,000 First World War veterans marched on Washington in the summer of 1932
findings.issue: The most authoritative and commonly cited figure for the Bonus Army is 43,000 total demonstrators (including 17,000 veterans plus families and affiliated groups), per Britannica and NPS. The National Parks Service and VA sources give 17,000 veterans specifically. '20,000 veterans' falls between these figures but does not match the most authoritative sources. The National Archives and Britannica consistently cite 17,000 veterans or 43,000 total. This is a minor point but could cause students to quote an inaccurate number.
findings.correction: The Bonus Army comprised approximately 43,000 total demonstrators, including around 17,000 World War One veterans plus their families and affiliated groups. Citing '20,000 veterans' is an approximation that does not match the most authoritative figures.

findings.lesson_title: Stalin's terror: purges, show trials and gulag
findings.claim: Nikolai Bukharin, once described by Lenin as 'the golden boy of the revolution.'
findings.issue: Lenin never used the phrase 'golden boy of the revolution' in his Testament or in any verified primary source. Lenin's Testament (1922–23) calls Bukharin 'not only a most valuable and major theorist of the Party' but also 'rightly considered the favourite of the whole Party' and criticises his scholastic grasp of dialectics. 'Golden boy of the revolution' is a popular secondary paraphrase found in journalism, not Lenin's words. Attributing it as Lenin's description is a misattribution.
findings.correction: Replace with Lenin's actual Testament wording: Bukharin was described by Lenin as 'the favourite of the whole Party' and 'the most valuable and biggest theoretician of the party', though Lenin also criticised his theoretical weaknesses. Do not attribute 'golden boy of the revolution' to Lenin.
findings.source: Lenin's Testament (Letter to the Congress, Dec 1922–Jan 1923): https://www.marxists.org/archive/lenin/works/1922/dec/testamnt/congress.htm

findings.lesson_title: The Great Patriotic War, 1941-1945
findings.claim: The Battle of Stalingrad lasted from August 1942 to February 1943 ... German forces under Field Marshal Paulus drove deep into the city
findings.issue: Paulus was not a Field Marshal during the Battle of Stalingrad. He held the rank of Generaloberst (Colonel-General) throughout the fighting. Hitler promoted him to Generalfeldmarschall (Field Marshal) on 31 January 1943 — the very day Paulus surrendered — as a signal that no German Field Marshal should surrender. The lesson's use of 'Field Marshal Paulus' in the context of driving into the city implies he held this rank during the battle, which is misleading.
findings.correction: Refer to him as 'General Paulus' (or 'Generaloberst Paulus') during the battle. His promotion to Field Marshal came only on the day of his surrender (31 January 1943). The surrender paragraph is separately accurate in calling him 'Paulus' without a title.

findings.lesson_title: The Home Front in the Second World War
findings.claim: The Coventry raid of 14 November 1940, in which over 500 bombers dropped incendiary and high-explosive bombs, destroyed the medieval city centre and killed approximately 554 people.
findings.issue: The figure of 554 does not appear in standard scholarly sources for this raid. The most widely cited figure in authoritative sources (Wikipedia, GCHQ, Historic Coventry, Coventry City Council) is approximately 568 killed. The International Churchill Society gives 507. No standard reference gives 554. The bomber figure of 'over 500' is within the range of sources (515–552) and is acceptable.
findings.correction: Replace '554' with 'approximately 568' (the most cited figure in standard historical references) or use 'approximately 500–570' to reflect the range across sources. Note that exact figures were never confirmed and differ across sources.
findings.source: Wikipedia Coventry Blitz: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry_Blitz; GCHQ: https://www.gchq.gov.uk/information/the-bombing-of-coventry-in-wwii; Historic Coventry: https://www.historiccoventry.co.uk/blitz/blitz.php?pg=stats

findings.lesson_title: Britain in the Twenties
findings.claim: Labour won 393 seats with 48 per cent of the vote [in 1945]
findings.issue: The 393 seats figure is correct. However, Labour's vote share in the 1945 election was approximately 47.7% (House of Commons Library) or 48.3% depending on source — not a clean '48 per cent'. More precisely, standard academic sources give 47.7% (UK Parliament/House of Commons Library). Stating '48 per cent' slightly overstates the share, though it is a rounding issue rather than a fabrication. This claim appears in lesson 4 (Post-war Britain) not lesson 1, but is flagged here as the most accurate lesson_id for the content.
findings.correction: Change '48 per cent' to 'approximately 48 per cent' or more precisely '47.7 per cent'. The 393 seats figure is correct.
findings.source: House of Commons Library UK Election Statistics 1918–2023: https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-7529/; Wikipedia 1945 election: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1945_United_Kingdom_general_election

findings.lesson_title: Post-war Britain, 1945-1960
findings.claim: Labour won 393 seats with 48 per cent of the vote.
findings.issue: The 393 seats figure is correct. Labour's actual vote share in 1945 was approximately 47.7% per the House of Commons Library, not a clean 48%. While minor, stating '48 per cent' is a rounding that slightly overstates Labour's share. Some sources give slightly different figures depending on how turnout and spoiled ballots are handled, but no authoritative source gives a clean 48.0%.
findings.correction: Change to 'approximately 48 per cent' or more accurately '47.7 per cent'. The seat count of 393 is correct.

findings.lesson_title: The Swinging Sixties
findings.claim: The Beatles, formed in Liverpool and achieving their first UK number one in 1963 with 'From Me to You'
findings.issue: This is defensible but contested. 'From Me to You' (April 1963) was the first Beatles single to reach No. 1 on the Record Retailer chart (now the Official UK Singles Chart). However, 'Please Please Me' (January 1963) reached No. 1 on multiple other contemporary charts (NME, Melody Maker, Disc). The lesson's phrasing is consistent with the modern Official Charts Company position, which retrospectively recognises 'From Me to You' as the first No. 1. This is not an error but worth noting the chart complexity if precision is needed.
findings.correction: The claim is acceptable per Official Charts Company. If precision is desired, add a qualifier: 'achieving their first UK number one on the official chart in 1963 with "From Me to You"' — noting that 'Please Please Me' topped several other contemporary charts.

findings.lesson_title: Nature of crimes: medieval and early modern
findings.claim: The Witchcraft Act of 1563, passed under Elizabeth I, made witchcraft a capital offence for the first time in England.
findings.issue: This is factually wrong on two counts. First, Henry VIII's Witchcraft Act of 1542 was the first English statute to make witchcraft a felony punishable by death (though it was repealed in 1547 by Edward VI). Second, the 1563 Act did NOT make all witchcraft a capital offence — it imposed the death penalty only for witchcraft causing death, and for second offences of lesser witchcraft. First offences causing injury (but not death) carried one year's imprisonment and pillory.
findings.correction: The 1563 Witchcraft Act was NOT the first to make witchcraft capital in England; Henry VIII's 1542 Act had already done so (repealed 1547). The 1563 Act also did not make all witchcraft capital — only witchcraft resulting in death (and repeat lesser offences). A more accurate formulation: 'The Witchcraft Act of 1563, passed under Elizabeth I, brought witchcraft under secular criminal law and imposed the death penalty for cases where the victim died, reviving and extending the approach of the repealed 1542 Act.'

findings.lesson_title: The birth of professional policing
findings.claim: The Metropolitan Police was established with approximately 3,200 officers organised on military lines
findings.issue: The initial operational strength of the Metropolitan Police when it took to the streets on 29 September 1829 was approximately 1,000 officers (specifically: 2 Commissioners, 8 Superintendents, 20 Inspectors, 88 Sergeants and 895 Constables = ~1,013). The force grew toward an authorised establishment approaching 3,000 by early 1830, but was not 3,200 at launch. Stating '3,200' as the founding number overstates the initial establishment and could mislead exam candidates.
findings.correction: The Metropolitan Police began with approximately 1,000 officers when it commenced patrols on 29 September 1829. The authorised establishment grew towards 3,000 by early 1830. The claim of '3,200 officers' at founding is not supported by primary sources.

findings.lesson_title: Methods of punishment: medieval to early modern
findings.claim: the theft of goods worth more than twelve pence (listed as an example of a Bloody Code capital offence, and again in the Key Fact box)
findings.issue: The threshold for capital theft under the Bloody Code is commonly cited as goods worth more than one shilling (12 pence = 1 shilling). This figure itself is contested and varied by context (grand larceny was historically over 12d), so the claim is not strictly wrong, but the lesson states 'twelve pence' without noting this equals one shilling — which could cause student confusion. More significantly, the lesson lists this as the Bloody Code threshold, which is broadly defensible for grand larceny as it stood at certain periods. Minor issue of imprecision rather than a clear factual error.
findings.correction: Theft of goods worth more than 12 pence (one shilling) was the historical grand larceny threshold. The lesson's figure is not wrong but noting '12 pence (one shilling)' would aid clarity for students.
findings.source: Standard legal-history sources on the Bloody Code; threshold of grand larceny traditionally 12d = 1 shilling.

findings.lesson_title: Public health: medieval to industrial
findings.claim: Cholera first struck Britain in 1831–1832 and returned in 1848–1849 and 1853–1854.
findings.issue: The third British cholera epidemic is conventionally dated 1853–1854, which is correct. However some authoritative sources date it 1853–1854 and others 1854 only (Snow's Broad Street investigation was 1854). The 1831–1832 and 1848–1849 dates are correct. No error here — this is accurate.
findings.correction: No correction needed; dates are accurate and consistent with mainstream scholarship. Low flag only to note the third epidemic is sometimes cited as 1853–1854 or simply 1854.

findings.lesson_title: Historic environment: Letchworth Garden City
findings.claim: it had no public house until 1962, when the Skittles Inn (a non-alcoholic tavern) was replaced by a conventional pub only after a local referendum
findings.issue: The Skittles Inn was NOT replaced by a pub in 1962. The Skittles Inn became the Settlement Adult Education Centre in 1925 — decades before the referendum. The first conventional licensed pub (the Broadway Hotel) opened in 1962 following a referendum held in 1957 (some sources say 1958). The Skittles Inn and the Broadway Hotel are separate buildings and events. The framing that the Skittles Inn was 'replaced' by a pub in 1962 conflates two unrelated events and is factually misleading.
findings.correction: Letchworth had no conventional public house until the Broadway Hotel opened in 1962, following a local referendum (held c.1957–1958). The Skittles Inn was a temperance tavern that had become the Settlement Adult Education Centre in 1925 — it was not 'replaced' by the Broadway Hotel. These are separate buildings and separate events separated by nearly 40 years.

findings.lesson_title: Historic environment: Letchworth Garden City
findings.claim: Letchworth itself was eventually taken into community ownership in 1962 when the Letchworth Garden City Corporation purchased the town from its shareholders.
findings.issue: The Letchworth Garden City Corporation did not 'purchase' the town from shareholders. Parliament passed the Letchworth Garden City Act 1962, which transferred the assets of First Garden City Ltd to a new statutory public corporation — this was a legislative compulsory transfer, not a market purchase. The trigger was that a private company (Hotel York Ltd) had been accumulating shares to take speculative control; Parliament intervened legislatively. The Corporation then formally took over on 1 January 1963 and paid agreed compensation of £3,115,000 to First Garden City Ltd. Saying 'purchased from shareholders' misstates the mechanism (it was a parliamentary forced transfer with compensation).
findings.correction: In 1962 Parliament passed the Letchworth Garden City Act, creating the Letchworth Garden City Corporation as a statutory public body and transferring the estate to it (effective 1 January 1963). This was a legislative compulsory transfer prompted by fears of speculative private takeover, not a commercial purchase from shareholders. Compensation of £3,115,000 was paid to First Garden City Ltd.

findings.lesson_title: Technology of warfare: medieval to industrial
findings.claim: The Maxim gun, developed by Hiram Maxim and adopted by the British army in 1884
findings.issue: 1884 is the year Maxim invented/demonstrated the gun, not when the British Army formally adopted it. The British Army first trialled it in 1885, placed an initial order of 120 in 1888/1889, and formally adopted the .303-calibre version in 1889.
findings.correction: The Maxim gun was invented by Hiram Maxim in 1884; it was adopted by the British Army in 1889 (initial order placed 1888).

findings.lesson_title: Historic environment: Royal Dockyards, Chatham c.1567-1984
findings.claim: The closure of Chatham, together with Sheerness and Deptford (both closed earlier in the nineteenth century)
findings.issue: Sheerness Dockyard did not close in the nineteenth century. It closed in 1959–1960 (announced February 1958, closed 1959). Only Deptford (1869) and Woolwich (1869) closed in the nineteenth century. Grouping Sheerness with Deptford as 'both closed earlier in the nineteenth century' is a factual error.
findings.correction: Sheerness Dockyard closed in 1959, not the nineteenth century. Deptford and Woolwich both closed in 1869. The correct statement should distinguish Sheerness (closed 1959) from Deptford/Woolwich (closed 1869).

findings.lesson_title: Historic environment: Glastonbury Festival c.1970 to the present day
findings.claim: T. Rex headlined in 1971; David Bowie played the Pyramid Stage in 1971 as well
findings.issue: T. Rex (Tyrannosaurus Rex) headlined the first festival in 1970, not 1971. T. Rex did not perform at the 1971 Glastonbury Fayre at all. The 1971 performers included David Bowie, Traffic, Fairport Convention, Hawkwind and others — but not T. Rex.
findings.correction: T. Rex (then billed as Tyrannosaurus Rex) headlined the 1970 Pilton Pop, Folk and Blues Festival, not 1971. The 1971 Glastonbury Fayre featured David Bowie (performing at dawn) but T. Rex did not appear.

findings.lesson_title: Holidays and travel over time
findings.claim: Legislation passed in 1871 that created four official public holidays in England, Wales and Ireland and two in Scotland
findings.issue: The Bank Holidays Act 1871 created four bank holidays in England, Wales and Ireland (Easter Monday, Whit Monday, first Monday in August, Boxing Day) but FIVE in Scotland (New Year's Day, Good Friday, first Monday in May, first Monday in August, Christmas Day) — not two.
findings.correction: The Bank Holidays Act 1871 created four public holidays in England, Wales and Ireland, and five in Scotland (New Year's Day, Good Friday, first Monday in May, first Monday in August, Christmas Day).

findings.lesson_title: Historic environment: Glastonbury Festival c.1970 to the present day
findings.claim: Fallow years occurred in 1991, 1996, 2001 (foot-and-mouth disease), 2006, 2012, and 2018
findings.issue: The list omits 1988, which was the first fallow year in the festival's history. The five-year cycle began after 1987, with 1988 as the first scheduled break.
findings.correction: Fallow years were: 1988 (first fallow year), 1991, 1996, 2001 (also foot-and-mouth), 2006, 2012, 2018, and then 2020–21 (COVID). The lesson's list omits 1988.
